title: Neuromyelitis optica and concomitant pulmonary tuberculosis: a case report
case_prompt: A 28-year-old Tunisian man with no prior medical history presented with a 7-day history of acute onset lower limb weakness and dysuria. Two months earlier, he developed dry cough, night sweats, anorexia, and weight loss that did not improve with broad-spectrum antibiotics. He reported no visual symptoms. On examination he was febrile, tachycardic, and fully conscious. Pulmonary auscultation revealed bilateral crepitations. Neurologic examination demonstrated complete paraplegia, decreased deep tendon reflexes, bilateral extensor plantar responses, a T4 sensory level, and urinary retention. Laboratory studies showed neutrophilic leukocytosis (white cells 15×10^9/L, neutrophils 11.8×10^9/L) and elevated C-reactive protein (62 mg/L). Serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative. MRI of the spine revealed an intramedullary tumefactive T2 hyperintensity extending from C5 to T10 with predominant gray matter involvement, bright spotty lesions, and multifocal heterogeneous enhancement on post-contrast images. Brain MRI showed T2 hyperintensity of the optic chiasm, enhancement of the right optic nerve and chiasm, and focal hyperintensity and enhancement of the left wall of the third ventricle in the hypothalamus; there were no tuberculomas, leptomeningeal enhancement, or vertebral lesions. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (7 cells/mm^3), elevated protein (3.23 g/L), and low glucose (1.9 mmol/L); oligoclonal bands were absent. Chest radiography and CT demonstrated diffuse reticulonodular infiltrates and left pulmonary excavations with air-fluid levels. The tuberculin skin test was positive, but sputum smear and culture for acid-fast bacilli were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Central nervous system tuberculosis was considered but ruled out because “First, mild pleiocytosis is not in line with the cellular formula found in the majority of cases with CNS involvement ... Secondly, glycorrhachia was only slightly decreased (1.9 mmol/l), and finally, MT-PCR on CSF was negative.”  
2. Pott’s disease was excluded since “CNS-MRI study did not show any sign in favor of infected intervertebral disc or bone destruction towards the diagnosis of Pott’s disease.”  
3. Tuberculous optic neuropathy was excluded as ocular tuberculosis signs were absent: “Papillitis, neuroretinitis, or optic nerve tuberculoma ... were not found in our patient ... Our patient had no posterior or panuveitis ... Finally, in CNS PT, ON mostly results from chronic papilledema due to meningitis, which was not the case in our patient.”  
4. Toxic optic neuritis from antitubercular drugs was ruled out because “Toxic neuritis due to isoniazid or ethambutol was also ruled out since ON was unilateral in our case.”
